I am 70 years old, and I have farmed the flat land of Quzhou County since I was a boy pulling a plow behind an ox. I never went to school, but I know this soil and this weather better than any book. I have six mu of land, which is enough for an old man to manage without breaking his back.

I do not try new crops anymore. At my age, I want crops I can trust and that do not need too much bending and pruning. Winter wheat and summer maize — that is the rotation my father did, and it is what I will do this year. The wheat is already in the ground from last October. Now that spring has come and the wheat is waking up, I will topdress it with urea at green-up and irrigate it four times: at green-up, jointing, heading, and grain filling. I will spray three times for weeds, insects, and rust. I use improved wheat seed from the township supply shop. It is not the old traditional seed, but it is not one of those fancy new names either. I expect about 900 jin per mu — not the highest in the village, but steady and enough.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant maize the same week without tilling. There is no need to turn the soil; I just plant the hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble. I put compound fertilizer down at planting and topdress once more when the stalks are knee-high. Two irrigations are usually enough in summer if the rains cooperate. I will spray for weeds and the corn borer three times. I hope to get about 1,100 jin per mu.

I stopped growing cotton years ago. My back cannot handle the pruning and all those sprays. Wheat and maize can be cut by machine, which saves these old bones. I keep enough wheat for my family’s flour and sell the rest. All the maize goes to the grain dealer who drives to the village. After the maize comes off in October, I will sow winter wheat again, just like every year. That is my life, and that is my plan.
